newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian court says no to "fiscal dictatorship".
newsitem.headline: Colombian court says no to "fiscal dictatorship".

text.p: Embattled Colombian President Ernesto Samper has suffered another major setback after a high court said he had no business ruling by decree over management of the country's troubled economy.

The Constitutional Court, in a 6-3 vote on Wednesday night, struck down all 16 decrees issued by the government under terms of an economic emergency it declared in January on grounds that they were unconstitutional and that the emergency itself could have been avoided.

The ruling came just hours after the government heralded approval of the economic emergency by both houses of Congress as a major political victory that would help it get its economic house in order and slash a yawning fiscal deficit that ran at 4 percent of gross domestic product last year.

But the court ruled that all of the problems relating to the fiscal deficit were foreseeable and not the result of unforeseen circumstances warranting emergency rule. In order to apply, the emergency measures must be approved by Congress on a case-by-case basis, it said, and not en masse as they were by lawmakers who merely empowered the government to rule by decree.

Business leaders had almost unanimously criticised the package of emergency measures, which included a 6 percent tax on all new foreign loans, as something that would drive up import costs, put inflationary pressure on the economy and hamper Colombia's economic liberalisation.

They had also bridled against the uncertainty it created since the government -- which has been severely weakened by the scandal stemming from Samper's alleged ties to drug lords -- had rammed through improvised measures without the prior approval of Congress.

"The court has called attention in this way to the possibility of opening the door to a fiscal dictatorship," said Sabas Pretelt de la Vega, president of the National Federation of Businessmen. The court, he added, had stopped the government from using the pretext of a state of emergency "to enact tax reforms that it can't get approved in Congress."
Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said the government would now seek to win congressional approval of all the measures it annnounced in January.

But in the meantime, it faces the likelihood of having to give back millions of dollars that it has collected since January through the new tax on foreign credits and a 16 percent sales tax on previously exempt services provided in Colombia by foreign-based companies.
The tax on foreign credits was aimed, in part, at avoiding a new surge in the peso, which strengthened substantially to the deteriment of exporters late last year on huge inflows of foreign capital.

To avoid another run up, now that the tax has been eliminated, the central bank hastily ruled on Wednesday night that 50 percent of any new foreign loans with a duration of less than five years must be deposited with the central bank for 18 months.

Economic analysts said the court ruling may ultimately have little impact since the government is widely expected to win approval for most of its emergency measures in Congress, which is dominated by Samper's Liberal Party.

The court seriously embarrassed the government, however, since it essentially disqualified what critics have long described as Samper's haphazard economic policy and came as a team of International Monetary Fund officials was visiting Bogota on an annual fact-finding mission.
"I seriously hope that these harsh economic measures will win support," Ocampo said. "There's nothing easy here when it comes to economic measures, everything's very difficult."
